title: Unloading and crashes
sub: Collectible contexts, what keeps them alive, and unhandled exceptions
cards/0/title: Collectible: a context you can unload
cards/0/body:
A context created with isCollectible: true can be unloaded together with all its assemblies (since .NET Core 3.0). The plugin code, its types and the machine code the JIT produced live in that context memory and are freed with it.

But unloading is cooperative. Unload() only starts it. The garbage collector finishes it, once no strong references from outside point at the context assemblies, types and objects, and no thread is running its code.

This is the opposite of AppDomain.Unload, which aborted threads by force. Here nobody aborts anything: whatever holds the context keeps it.
cards/0/deep: Inside the runtime the context memory belongs to a LoaderAllocator object. While it is reachable, nothing is freed. Limitations: C++/CLI assemblies cannot be loaded into a collectible context, and ReadyToRun machine code in such assemblies is ignored, so the JIT compiles the methods.
cards/1/q: The alc.Unload() call has returned. Are the plugin assemblies unloaded already?
cards/1/options/0: No: unloading has only started, the GC finishes it once no references remain
cards/1/options/2: Yes, and the plugin threads are aborted, as with AppDomain
cards/1/options/3: No: a collectible context unloads only at process exit
cards/1/explain: Unload puts the context into the unloading state. Only the garbage collector can free the memory, and it does so when the context becomes unreachable.
cards/1/wrong/2: AppDomain unloaded by force. AssemblyLoadContext aborts nobody: a thread running plugin code keeps the context alive.
cards/2/body:
Unloading is blocked by any strong reference from outside to an assembly, type or object of the context, and by context code on the stack of any thread. In practice:

  • host static fields and caches: a Type → handler dictionary, the last plugin result;
  • subscriptions: the plugin subscribed to a host event, so the event delegate references the plugin object;
  • plugin threads and timers: a thread in Thread.Sleep, a Timer, a RegisteredWaitHandle with a plugin callback;
  • strong GCHandles, normal and pinned;
  • local variables, including invisible temporaries the JIT introduced;
  • fields of your AssemblyLoadContext subclass that reference plugin assemblies and objects.

A WeakReference does not block unloading.
cards/2/deep: The last item is sneaky: while unloading is in progress, the runtime itself holds a strong handle to the context object. So subclass fields pointing at an Assembly or plugin objects will not be collected even after you let go of the context. Clear them. The AssemblyLoadContext.Unloading event is where a plugin can stop its threads and free its GCHandles.
cards/3/q: What will prevent the plugin context from unloading? Select all.
cards/3/options/0: A host static field holds a plugin object
cards/3/options/1: The plugin subscribed to a static host event
cards/3/options/2: A plugin background thread sleeps in Thread.Sleep
cards/3/options/3: The host keeps a WeakReference to the context
cards/3/options/4: The plugin passed a string to the host, and the host stored it
cards/3/explain: A static field and a delegate in an event are strong references to a plugin object. A sleeping thread keeps plugin code on its stack. A WeakReference does not count. A string is a System.String from CoreLib, not a plugin type: it does not hold the context.
cards/4/title: How to unload and make sure
cards/4/body:
Everything that touches the plugin goes into a separate method marked NoInlining: otherwise the JIT may inline it into the caller, and references to the context stay in the caller stack. Only a WeakReference is handed out.

Then you run garbage collection while the reference is alive. One pass is usually enough. If plugin objects have finalizers, it takes several: a finalizer keeps its object alive for one more collection.
cards/4/deep: If the context does not unload, take a dump and find what holds it. In WinDbg or LLDB with the SOS extension, dumpheap -type LoaderAllocator shows the context object and gcroot <address> shows the reference chain to a root. The root can be a stack slot, a static field or a GCHandle. If a thread running plugin code holds the context, the thread stacks show it (clrstack).
cards/5/q: After RunPlugin and the GC.Collect loop the context is still alive. Registry is a static host class. Which line blocks unloading?
cards/5/explain: A host static field is a GC root. Through the plugin object it holds its type, its assembly and the whole context. The method locals disappear after it returns; the static field does not.
cards/6/title: An unhandled exception: the process goes down
cards/6/body:
An exception nobody catches terminates the whole process, whatever thread it happens on: the main thread, a new Thread, the thread pool, the finalizer thread.

Then: in .NET Framework 1.x exceptions on pool threads and the finalizer were silently swallowed, and only the thread died. Version 2.0 made the policy strict, and the legacyUnhandledExceptionPolicy flag in app.config brought the old behavior back. Modern .NET has no such flag.

Why: a thread that dies quietly leaves program state half-changed, and the program goes on with corrupted data. Better to fail at once and loudly.
cards/6/deep: The runtime itself swallows only the service exceptions it uses to control threads: in Framework, ThreadAbortException and AppDomainUnloadedException on threads the CLR created. In .NET 5+ Thread.Abort throws PlatformNotSupportedException. A stack overflow cannot be caught at all: the process ends without events or finally blocks; the stack lesson in the memory course covers it.
cards/7/q: The host calls plugin.Run() inside try/catch (Exception). Inside Run the plugin does new Thread(() => throw new InvalidOperationException()).Start() and returns at once. What happens?
cards/7/options/0: The process terminates: nobody caught the exception on the other thread
cards/7/options/1: The host catch catches the exception
cards/7/options/2: Only the plugin thread dies, the host keeps running
cards/7/explain: try/catch catches only exceptions of its own thread. The new thread has no handler, so the exception becomes unhandled, and that terminates the whole process. An assembly load context does not protect against crashes.
cards/7/wrong/2: That was .NET Framework 1.x. Since 2.0 an unhandled exception on any thread terminates the process.
cards/8/title: UnhandledException is a notice, not a rescue
cards/8/body:
The AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException event arrives before termination. In it you can write a log, flush buffers, save a dump. You cannot cancel the crash: e.IsTerminating is true.

What does not bring the process down:

  • an exception in a Task nobody awaited: since .NET 4.5 it only raises TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException when the GC collects the task;
  • an exception caught in a catch.

But async void does crash it: the exception has nowhere to return, so it is thrown on the synchronization context or the thread pool.
cards/8/deep:
.NET 10 added ExceptionHandling.SetUnhandledExceptionHandler(Func<Exception, bool>) in System.Runtime.ExceptionServices. The documentation names its purpose: hosts such as REPLs and game scripting that cannot otherwise handle exceptions thrown by plugins. The handler returns true if the exception was handled, and it can be set once; a second call throws InvalidOperationException. Check the documentation for your version on which threads and cases it covers before building a host on it.

In .NET Framework a native host could change the policy through ICLRPolicyManager::SetUnhandledExceptionPolicy.
cards/9/q: What terminates the process by default in .NET 8? Select all.
cards/9/options/0: An exception in a method started with new Thread
cards/9/options/1: An exception in an async void method
cards/9/options/2: An exception in a Task nobody awaited
cards/9/options/3: An exception in a ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem callback
cards/9/options/4: An exception caught in catch and logged
cards/9/explain: A thread, async void and a pool callback have no handler above them, so the exception becomes unhandled. A task nobody awaited only raises UnobservedTaskException during garbage collection.
cards/10/title: Summary: what a plugin context protects against
cards/10/body:
It protects against dependency version conflicts, and it lets you unload a plugin and load a new version without a restart.

It does not protect against crashes, since an exception on a plugin thread terminates the host; against memory corruption and infinite loops, since the heap and the CPU are shared; against leaks, since a forgotten subscription holds the whole context.

A plugin you do not trust, or one that crashes often, needs a separate process: you can kill it, restart it and cap its memory with OS tools. That is what replaces what domains used to do.
cards/11/q: The host subscribed to UnhandledException and writes a log in the handler. A plugin timer throws an exception in its callback. What happens?
cards/11/options/0: The log is written, then the process terminates
cards/11/options/1: The log is written, and the host keeps running
cards/11/options/2: The handler is not called: the exception is from another context
cards/11/options/3: The timer stops, everything else keeps running
cards/11/explain: A timer callback runs on the thread pool, and an exception in it becomes unhandled. The UnhandledException event is process-wide: it arrives, but it cannot cancel termination.
cards/11/wrong/2: Load contexts do not split the process into domains. There is one UnhandledException event for the whole process.
